title: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE WHEN WE’RE AFRAID… BUT RARELY UNDERSTAND
paragraphs: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE WHEN WE’RE AFRAID… BUT RARELY UNDERSTAND

Romans 8:31 does not promise that nobody will fight you. It promises something far more terrifying to your enemies, more comforting to the wounded, and more glorious than an easy life: if you belong to Jesus Christ, nothing that comes against you can overturn what God has determined to accomplish for you in Christ.
You have probably heard the verse when somebody was trying to encourage you.
Maybe you were afraid.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe everything you worked for was collapsing.
Maybe you were sitting alone after midnight, staring at a ceiling while your mind rehearsed every possible way your life could fall apart.
And somewhere in the middle of the fear, someone said:
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
It sounds powerful.
Almost invincible.
But there is a problem.
People can be against you.
Very much against you.
They can reject you.
Lie about you.
Abandon you.
Misunderstand you.
Mock your faith.
Break promises.
Close doors.
Damage your reputation.
Take advantage of your kindness.
And sometimes the person fighting against your peace is the person staring back at you in the mirror.
So what did Paul mean?
Was Romans 8:31 merely religious motivation?
Was he saying Christians become untouchable?
Was he promising that believers will always win the court case, get the promotion, defeat the sickness, escape suffering, silence their critics, and eventually watch every enemy regret opposing them?
No.
And somehow, the real meaning is even better.
Paul writes in Romans 8:31:
Ti oun eroumen pros tauta? Ei ho Theos hyper hēmōn, tis kath’ hēmōn?
A faithful rendering is:
“What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Notice the question Paul does not ask.
He does not ask, “Who will ever oppose us?”
He asks, in effect, what opposition can ultimately prevail when God Himself is for His people?
That difference changes everything.
The Greek expression ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν — hyper hēmōn means “for us,” “on our behalf,” or “in our interest.”
And Paul does not leave “God is for us” floating in the air as a motivational slogan.
He proves it.
The very next verse says:
“ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο…”
“He who did not spare His own Son…”
There is the foundation.
Not your bank account.
Not your popularity.
Not your circumstances.
Not whether everybody likes you.
Not whether your plans succeeded this year.
Not whether the door opened.
Not whether your body feels strong.
Not whether your family finally understands you.
Paul points to a cross.
God being “for us” does not mean God gives us everything our frightened hearts demand.
It means God has already given the greatest gift He could give:
His Son.
And suddenly Romans 8:31 becomes much deeper than the inspirational quote printed on a coffee mug.
Because some of us have secretly interpreted “God is for me” to mean:
“God will make my life go the way I want.”
Paul means something infinitely greater:
God has acted decisively for sinners through Jesus Christ, and no created power can finally overthrow His saving purpose for those who are in Christ.
That matters because Romans 8 begins in a courtroom.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Think about that.
The chapter that eventually asks, “Who can be against us?” begins by dealing with the greatest thing that was against us.
Our guilt.
Our sin.
Our condemnation.
Before you worry about the person who betrayed you, there was a deeper problem.
Before the diagnosis.
Before the divorce papers.
Before the rejection.
Before the financial disaster.
Before the nights when anxiety would not let you sleep.
Humanity’s deepest problem was never merely that painful circumstances were against us.
Sin was against us.
The righteous judgment of God against sin was real.
And we could not rescue ourselves.
We did not need better self-esteem.
We needed reconciliation.
We did not merely need encouragement.
We needed redemption.
We did not merely need God to improve our circumstances.
We needed God to save us.
And this is where the scandal becomes grace.
God did not look at guilty sinners and pretend sin did not matter.
He did something unimaginably costly.
Romans 8:3 says God sent “His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin” and condemned sin in the flesh.
Jesus Christ stepped into our world.
The sinless One came for sinners.
The innocent One was rejected.
The righteous One suffered.
The beloved Son went to the cross.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine and needed inspiration.
He died because sin is devastatingly serious—and because the love of God is astonishingly deep.
At Calvary, grace was not God shrugging His shoulders at evil.
Grace was costly.
Christ bore what sinners could never repair by religious performance.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now the person trusting in Christ can hear Romans 8:31 differently.
“If God is for us…”
Not because we were impressive enough.
Not because we prayed perfectly.
Not because we never fell again.
Not because we finally became respectable enough for God to tolerate.
God is for His people because their hope rests in Christ.
Somebody needs to hear that slowly.
Because you may have spent years believing God loves the cleaned-up version of you.
The version who remembers to pray.
The version who never loses patience.
The version who does not struggle with temptation.
The version who does not wake up discouraged.
The version who has answers.
The version who smiles at church.
But you know the other version too.
The version nobody sees.
The thoughts you would never put on Facebook.
The private shame.
The recurring temptation.
The memory you wish you could erase.
The prayer you stopped praying because disappointment exhausted you.
The thing you promised God you would never do again.
And then you did it again.
You may have wondered:
“How could God possibly still want me?”
Romans 8 does not answer by telling you to stare harder at yourself.
It turns your eyes toward Christ.
Listen to Paul’s next question:
“Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?”
Then:
“It is God who justifies.”
And then:
“Who is to condemn?”
Paul answers by pointing directly to Jesus Christ—the One who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and intercedes for His people.
Do you see what Paul is doing?
He keeps asking courtroom questions.
Who can successfully prosecute those whom God justifies?
Who can deliver a final condemning verdict against the person whose hope is in the crucified and risen Christ?
Satan may accuse.
People may accuse.
Your memories may accuse.
Your own conscience may remind you of sins you genuinely committed.
Christianity does not require pretending those sins never happened.
The Gospel announces something better:
Jesus died for sinners.
Repentance does not mean calling darkness light.
It means bringing darkness into the light and running toward the mercy of Christ.
Grace is not permission to keep loving sin.
Grace is the undeserved mercy that receives the repentant sinner and begins transforming the person who could never transform himself.
This is why “God is for us” cannot biblically mean “nothing painful will happen.”
Look at what Paul says only a few sentences later.
He speaks about tribulation.
Distress.
Persecution.
Famine.
Nakedness.
Danger.
Sword.
Those words destroy the prosperity-gospel interpretation of Romans 8:31.
Paul does not say:
“If God is for you, there will be no tribulation.”
He essentially says:
Tribulation may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Distress may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Persecution may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Loss may come.
Tears may come.
Funerals may come.
Opposition may come.
And Christians are not promised exemption from every earthly tragedy.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would face trouble.
The apostles suffered.
Paul suffered.
Faithful believers throughout history have suffered.
So Romans 8:31 is not a divine promise that every battle ends the way you wanted.
It is the announcement that no battle can finally overthrow the saving purpose of God in Christ.
That is much stronger.
Because a faith built on “God will prevent anything painful from happening to me” collapses the moment pain arrives.
But a faith anchored in the crucified and risen Jesus can whisper through tears:
“This hurts…
but Christ has not abandoned me.”
That is Romans 8 faith.
It is possible for something to hurt you without ultimately defeating God’s purpose for you.
It is possible for someone to reject you without changing your standing in Christ.
It is possible to lose something precious without losing Jesus.
It is possible to walk through a season you never would have chosen and discover that the presence of God is not measured by the absence of suffering.
And there is another detail we often overlook.
Paul asks:
“What then shall we say to these things?”
What things?
Look backward.
Romans 8 has already spoken about suffering.
It says creation groans.
Believers groan.
We wait.
We hope.
We experience weakness.
Sometimes we do not even know what we ought to pray.
That may be one of the most human sentences in the Bible.
There are moments when pain becomes too complicated for polished prayers.
You sit there.
You try to speak.
Nothing comes.
Maybe only tears.
Maybe only:
“Jesus…”
And Romans 8 says the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
God’s faithfulness toward His children does not depend upon their ability to manufacture impressive spiritual emotions.
Then comes Romans 8:28, another verse frequently removed from its context:
“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose.”
Paul is not saying all things are good.
Betrayal is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Sin is not secretly holy because God can redeem broken situations.
Evil remains evil.
But evil does not become sovereign.
That belongs to God.
The astonishing Christian hope is that God is so sovereign, wise, and faithful that even what He hates and what wounds us cannot finally frustrate His redemptive purpose.
And what is the “good” toward which Romans 8 is moving?
The next verse tells us.
Those God foreknew He also predestined “to be conformed to the image of His Son.”
There it is.
Sometimes we define “good” as comfortable.
God is making His people like Jesus.
We define “good” as getting what we wanted.
God is preparing a redeemed people for glory.
We define “God is for me” as God supporting every personal ambition.
Scripture defines God’s saving purpose around Christ.
That means there may be moments when God’s faithfulness does not look like the answer you requested.
Sometimes the door stays closed.
Sometimes the relationship ends.
Sometimes healing does not come in the timing we desperately wanted.
Sometimes obedience costs something.
Sometimes following Jesus means losing the approval of people whose approval once controlled you.
But if you are in Christ, your story is not ultimately being written by rejection.
Or shame.
Or failure.
Or suffering.
Or your worst chapter.
Jesus Christ has entered the story.
And Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
That is why Romans 8 eventually explodes into one of the greatest declarations of Christian assurance ever written:
“For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers…”
Paul keeps going.
Height.
Depth.
Anything else in all creation.
None of it “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Read those last words again.
In Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is the center.
Romans 8:31 is not ultimately a celebration of how unstoppable you are.
It is a celebration of how sufficient Christ is.
Christian confidence is not:
“Nobody can touch me.”
It is:
“Nothing can separate me from Jesus.”
Not:
“I will never lose.”
But:
“Christ has already conquered sin and death, and my ultimate hope is secured in Him.”
Not:
“My enemies will eventually watch me become successful.”
But:
“My identity is no longer determined by the verdict of my enemies.”
Maybe that is the freedom you actually needed.
Because some of us have been living as defendants in a courtroom God already dismissed.
Still trying to prove ourselves.
Still arguing with voices from ten years ago.
Still checking whether the people who rejected us finally recognize our worth.
Still hoping success will make somebody regret how they treated us.
Still fantasizing about the day we can say:
“Look at me now.”
But what if grace is calling you somewhere better?
What if healing is not finally making them regret losing you?
What if healing is reaching the point where Jesus is enough even if they never apologize?
What if freedom is no longer needing your enemies to lose before you can believe God loves you?
That changes the verse.
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
People can be against you.
But they cannot become God.
Your past can testify against you.
But your past cannot crucify Jesus twice and reverse His finished work.
Suffering can shake you.
But suffering cannot dethrone Christ.
Death itself can take a believer’s earthly breath.
But death cannot separate the believer from the love of God in Christ.
That is the audacity of Romans 8.
The Christian is not promised an opponent-free life.
The Christian is promised a Christ-secured hope.
And maybe you are reading this while fighting something nobody knows about.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
You have learned how to answer, “I’m okay.”
You know how to post the photograph.
You know how to laugh at the right moment.
You know how to worship while your heart feels exhausted.
But somewhere beneath all of it is a question you have been afraid to ask:
“God… are You still for me?”
If you belong to Jesus, do not measure the answer by today’s circumstances.
Look toward Calvary.
“He who did not spare His own Son…”
The cross is not evidence that Christians never suffer.
The cross itself proves otherwise.
The cross is evidence that God’s saving love goes deeper than suffering.
And the empty tomb announces that suffering and death do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Perhaps you have never actually surrendered to Him.
You know verses.
You know Christian language.
Maybe you even share Christian posts.
But Christianity is not ultimately sharing religious content.
You can own a Bible and never surrender.
You can attend church while secretly building your identity around everything except Christ.
Romans 8:31 is not permission to assume God endorses us regardless of our relationship to His Son.
The magnificent assurance of Romans 8 belongs within the Gospel reality Paul repeatedly describes as being “in Christ.”
So do not merely admire the promise.
Come to the Savior at the center of it.
Repent.
Stop defending the sin Jesus died to save you from.
Bring Him the secret.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The sexual sin.
The resentment.
The double life.
The religious performance.
The thing you keep hiding because you are terrified of what happens when the light reaches it.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is grace for sinners.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new life that does not begin with pretending you were never broken but with confessing that you desperately need a Savior.
Not because a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing a confession into the light begins with refusing to hide behind another polished Christian response.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer walking through a battle.
Let the body of Christ behave like the body of Christ.
Pray for one another.
Carry one another.
Remind one another where hope actually lives.
And then think of one person who needs Romans 8 tonight.
Not the person who will merely “like” it.
The person whose faith is hanging by a thread.
The person going through a divorce.
The father terrified about his family.
The mother crying where her children cannot see her.
The believer ashamed of falling again.
The friend who thinks suffering means God abandoned them.
The skeptic who believes Christianity is nothing more than motivational religion.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not. Salvation cannot be purchased, and the glory of God cannot be reduced to an engagement metric.

If this ministry is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent more deeply, heal biblically, and stand stronger in the Gospel, one practical way you can help us glorify God together is by helping that truth travel farther than it could travel without you.
Your share may enter a home we could never enter.
Your tag may reach someone we could never identify.
Your comment may encourage someone who thought they were struggling alone.
Your support can help Gospel-centered resources continue reaching believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, wounded Christians, and even unbelievers who desperately need to hear about Jesus.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.

But it can be a practical way of supporting a ministry that is committed to spreading Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, conviction, discipleship, healing, repentance, and the message of redemption through Jesus Christ.
And there is something bigger than merchandise behind the invitation.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never forgive what they have done.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions nobody has taken seriously.
Because eventually you may have a day when Romans 8:31 feels harder to believe than it does right now.
On that day, come back.
Read the context again.
Remember:
Paul never promised that nobody would stand against you.
He promised something better.
They cannot overturn the verdict of the God who justifies.
They cannot separate you from the Christ who died and rose.
They cannot transform suffering into sovereign power over your eternity.
They cannot erase the cross.
They cannot seal the tomb again.
They cannot dethrone Jesus.
And if Christ has you, even death itself cannot carry you somewhere His love cannot reach.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Because the greatest news in Romans 8 is not that you finally became strong enough to defeat everything against you.
The greatest news is that when you had no hope of saving yourself, God gave His Son.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ intercedes.
Christ holds His people.
And Christ will have the final word.
So when tomorrow comes against you…
when fear comes against you…
when accusation comes against you…
when temptation comes against you…
when disappointment comes against you…
when grief comes against you…
when your own trembling heart begins whispering that perhaps God has forgotten your name…
do not answer by pointing to how strong you are.
Point to the cross.
Point to the empty tomb.
Point to Jesus.
And whisper the truth the enemy desperately wants suffering to make you forget:
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Not because nobody will try.
But because nobody can finally defeat the saving purpose of the God who gave His Son for His people.
Your darkest chapter may still bear the scars of what happened—but scars are not proof that Jesus abandoned the story; sometimes they are the very place where grace leaves its signature.
